name: AI Donor Analytics
objectives: Given a donor list, make an anonymous working copy with names replaced by IDs and contact details deleted, keeping only ID, gift date, amount and campaign

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Getting your donor data ready, safely
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Make a clean, anonymous copy of a donor list that is safe to analyze.
This lesson builds toward: Given a donor list, you will make an anonymous working copy with names replaced by IDs and contact details deleted, keeping only ID, gift date, amount and campaign.
Donor analytics means looking at your giving records to learn who gives, how much, how often and whether they come back. You only need a spreadsheet.
Donor names, addresses, emails and gift amounts are private and must be protected. Before you analyze anything with AI, make a copy and replace each name with an ID like D001. Delete addresses, phone numbers, emails and notes. Keep only the ID, gift date, gift amount and, if you have it, the campaign or fund.
Keep the real list in your donor system or a protected file. The anonymous copy is what you work with. Follow your organization's privacy policy and any promises you made to donors.
Step by step:
- Export or copy your donor list into a spreadsheet.
- Save a separate copy named "donors-anonymous".
- Replace each name with an ID such as D001, D002.
- Delete addresses, phone numbers, emails and notes.
- Keep only ID, gift date, amount and campaign.
Words to know:
- Donor analytics: studying giving records to learn who gives, how much, how often and whether they return.
- Anonymous: with names and contact details removed so no one can tell who is who.
- Spreadsheet: a table of rows and columns, like Google Sheets or Microsoft Excel.
Try it now: Make a practice list in a spreadsheet with 12 rows: ID (D001 to D010, some repeated), gift date (last year and this year) and amount. Or make an anonymous copy of your real list following the steps.
You can now prepare a donor list that is safe to analyze, with names and contact details removed.

check.q: What do you delete from the anonymous copy?
options: Addresses, phone numbers, emails and notes
check.why: Delete contact details and notes; keep ID, date, amount and campaign.

check.q: A volunteer wants to analyze the real donor list on their personal laptop. What do you do?
options: Give them the anonymous copy and keep the real list in the protected file
Print the real list for them
Paste the real list into AI for them
check.why: Keep the real list protected; work with the anonymous copy.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Three numbers every nonprofit should know
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Calculate total raised, average gift and donor retention rate.
This lesson builds toward: Given an anonymous donor spreadsheet, you will calculate total raised, average gift and donor retention rate, getting each number right.
Total raised is all gifts added together. Average gift is total raised divided by the number of gifts. In a spreadsheet, =SUM() adds a column and =AVERAGE() gives the average.
Donor retention rate tells you how many of last year's donors gave again this year. Count the donors who gave last year. Count how many of those also gave this year. Divide the second number by the first and multiply by 100. If 40 donors gave last year and 18 of them gave again, retention is 18 / 40 = 45 percent.
Retention matters because keeping a donor usually costs less than finding a new one. A low rate is a sign to thank and update donors better.
Step by step:
- Total raised: =SUM() of the amount column.
- Average gift: =AVERAGE() of the amount column.
- Count unique donors who gave last year.
- Count how many of them also gave this year.
- Retention = this-year repeat donors / last-year donors x 100.
Words to know:
- Average gift: total raised divided by the number of gifts.
- Retention rate: the percent of last year's donors who gave again this year.
- Formula: a calculation typed into a spreadsheet cell, starting with =.
Try it now: Using your practice or anonymous list, calculate total raised, average gift and retention rate. Write the three numbers down.
You can now calculate total raised, average gift and donor retention rate in a spreadsheet.

check.q: Which formula adds up a column of gifts?
check.why: =SUM() adds a column; =AVERAGE() gives the average.

check.q: 20 donors gave last year and 10 of them gave again. What is your retention rate?

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Grouping donors into segments
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Sort donors into simple groups so each group gets the right message.
This lesson builds toward: Given your donor IDs and gift history, you will sort donors into New, Repeat, Lapsed and Larger segments and count each group, with every donor ID in a segment.
A segment is a group of donors who are alike in a way that matters. Different groups need different messages.
Simple segments to start: New donors (first gift this year), Repeat donors (gave last year and this year), Lapsed donors (gave last year but not this year), and Larger donors (gifts above an amount you choose, such as your top 10 percent).
Add a column called Segment and fill it in for each donor ID. You can use the spreadsheet's filter or sort to group them. Count how many donors are in each group.
Step by step:
- Add a column called Segment.
- Mark each donor ID as New, Repeat, Lapsed or Larger.
- Use sort or filter to group them.
- Count the donors in each group.
Words to know:
- Segment: a group of donors who are alike in a way that matters, like new or lapsed.
- Lapsed donor: someone who gave before but has not given this year.
Try it now: Add a Segment column to your list. Mark every donor ID and count how many are New, Repeat, Lapsed and Larger.
You can now sort donors into segments and count each group.

check.q: Which segment is a donor who gave last year and this year?
check.why: Repeat donors gave last year and this year.

check.q: You want to see all lapsed donors together. What do you do in the spreadsheet?
options: Retype them on a new page
Use the filter or sort on the Segment column
check.why: Use the spreadsheet's filter or sort to group them.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Using AI to explain your numbers
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Ask an AI assistant to explain anonymous donor numbers in plain words.
This lesson builds toward: Given your summary numbers, you will ask an AI assistant to explain them in plain words and recheck any math or benchmark it gives, pasting only summary numbers, never the donor list.
You can paste your summary numbers, not your donor list, into an AI assistant such as ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot or Google Gemini and ask what they mean.
For example: "I run a small food bank. Last year 40 donors, this year 35. Retention 45 percent. Average gift $85. Segments: 17 new, 18 repeat, 22 lapsed, 4 larger. Explain what these numbers tell me in plain words and what questions I should ask next."
AI can also suggest formulas or chart types if you get stuck. Check any math it does yourself; AI can make arithmetic mistakes and can make up benchmark numbers that sound real.
Step by step:
- Write your summary numbers, not individual donors.
- Say what kind of organization you are.
- Ask the AI to explain the numbers in plain words.
- Ask what questions you should ask next.
- Recheck any math yourself.
Words to know:
- Summary numbers: totals, averages and counts, not information about any one person.
- Benchmark: a typical number used for comparison; AI may make these up, so check the source.
Try it now: Paste only your summary numbers (totals, retention, average gift, segment counts) into an AI assistant and ask it to explain them and suggest three questions to ask next.
You can now use an AI assistant to explain donor numbers without sharing any donor's private information.

check.q: Besides explaining numbers, what else can AI help with in this lesson?
check.why: AI can suggest formulas or chart types if you get stuck.

check.q: AI says your average gift is $95, but your spreadsheet says $85. What do you do?
options: Ask AI to agree with you
Recheck the math yourself and use the correct number
check.why: AI can make arithmetic mistakes, so check its math yourself.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Making a simple chart
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Make one chart that shows your donor segments clearly.
This lesson builds toward: Given your segment counts, you will create a bar chart with a clear title in Google Sheets or Excel, showing one message.
A chart helps your board and team see the story fast. A bar chart works well for segments: one bar each for New, Repeat, Lapsed and Larger.
In Google Sheets or Excel, put the segment names in one column and the counts in the next. Select both columns, then use the Insert menu to add a chart and choose a bar or column chart.
Give the chart a clear title like "Our donors this year by group". Keep it simple: one message per chart.
Step by step:
- Make a small table: segment name and count.
- Select both columns.
- Insert a chart and choose a bar or column chart.
- Give it a clear title.
- Check the numbers match your table.
Words to know:
- Bar chart: a chart that compares amounts using bars of different lengths.
Try it now: Make a bar chart of your four segment counts with a clear title.
You can now make a clear bar chart of donor segments for your team or board.

check.q: What do you select before inserting a chart?
options: The segment names and their counts
The whole donor list with names
check.why: Select the segment names column and the counts column, then insert the chart.

check.q: Your chart tries to show segments, gift sizes and months all at once. What do you do?
options: Keep it to one message per chart
check.why: Keep it simple: one message per chart.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Turning findings into an appeal plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write a one-page plan with one action for each donor segment.
This lesson builds toward: Given your findings, you will write a one-page appeal plan with one action, owner and date for each segment, using placeholders for donor names and checked with your director.
Numbers matter only if they change what you do. For each segment, choose one action. New donors: a warm welcome and a story about what their gift did. Repeat donors: a thank-you and an invitation to give monthly. Lapsed donors: a "we miss you" note with an update. Larger donors: a personal call or visit from a leader.
AI can draft each message. Use placeholders like [donor name] and [program result], then fill them in yourself in your donor system or mail merge.
Write a one-page plan: your three key numbers, the chart, one action per segment, who does it and by when. Check it with your director before you send anything. Follow any rules your organization has about donor contact and opt-outs.
Step by step:
- Write your three key numbers at the top.
- Add your chart.
- Choose one action per segment.
- Ask AI to draft each message with placeholders.
- Add who does what and by when, and get approval.
Words to know:
- Appeal: a request asking supporters to give.
- Mail merge: a tool that fills each letter or email with one person's details from a list.
Try it now: Final task: write your one-page appeal plan with your three numbers, chart, one action per segment and owners. Ask AI to draft the "we miss you" note with placeholders, then edit it in your own words.
You can now turn donor numbers into a practical appeal plan that respects donor privacy.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Safe copy A name, address, phone, email or note is still in the copy. Names replaced by IDs; only ID, date, amount and campaign kept. Notes where the real list is kept and who can open it. Key numbers Retention rate or average gift is calculated wrong. Total raised, average gift and retention rate are all correct. Shows the formula or working for each number. Donor segments Fewer than three groups, or donors left out. At least three segments, every donor ID in one, with counts. Uses all four segments, with a stated amount for Larger donors. AI explanation checked Donor-level data was pasted, or AI math or benchmarks were used unchecked. Only summary numbers pasted; AI's math and any benchmark rechecked. Lists the questions AI suggested asking next and the answers. Appeal plan No action for a segment, or no owner or date. One page with key numbers, chart, one action per segment, owner and date. Draft messages use placeholders and the plan is approved by the director. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What is a good action for new donors?
options: Ask them to give monthly right away
A warm welcome and a story about what their gift did
check.why: New donors get a warm welcome and a story about what their gift did.

check.q: Your appeal plan is written. What do you do before sending anything?
options: Send it to every donor at once
Check it with your director and follow your donor contact and opt-out rules
check.why: Check with your director and follow your rules on donor contact and opt-outs.
